title: Who Are You Giving a Halo To
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece explains the halo effect, the cognitive bias in which one strongly favorable impression of a person distorts a leader's judgment of everything else about them. The author notes that team members can see this bias clearly even when the leader can't, watching a favored colleague get a free pass while others' concerns go unheard. It also addresses the reverse halo, where an early negative impression colors every subsequent judgment of a person unfairly. Both distortions, the piece argues, damage the candid dialogue that healthy teams depend on. Leaders are urged to evaluate people's traits independently rather than as a single, undifferentiated impression.
points: The halo effect causes leaders to rate every trait of a favored person positively, based on one strong impression.
Team members notice a leader's halo bias even when the leader is unaware of it.
A reverse halo works the opposite way, unfairly coloring every judgment of a disfavored person negatively.
Good leaders evaluate people's traits independently rather than as one undifferentiated impression.
quotes: This bias for leaders is so strong at times that they go out of their way to dispute, ignore, or dismiss negative information and data about people they think highly of.
This wreaks havoc on the candid and open dialogue which is essential for cohesive teams.
While everyone deserves your support and positivity, no one is worthy of a halo.
Any time a leader views a colleague in a highly favorable way and then proceeds to evaluate everything else about them as positive, they are said to be giving that person a halo .
Once given a Halo, these colleagues can do little wrong in the eyes of the leader.
Technically speaking, the so-called halo effect is a cognitive bias whereby people overestimate the specific qualities of a person because of an extremely favorable general impression.
The halo they attach to others creates a powerful distortion, influencing how they interpret many other features and descriptions about the person.
This distortion is rampant in everyday judgments of people, and leaders are especially susceptible to it.
